screens.title: Game Project Structure and Version Control
screens.narratorSegment: Today we take two essential steps that keep a game project healthy over time. First, you will learn how to organize Godot project files so you and your team can find scenes, assets, and scripts quickly. A consistent layout prevents confusion, reduces accidental edits, and speeds development. Second, you will learn how to use Git to record your project's history, share work with others, and recover from mistakes. We’ll walk through initializing a repository, configuring a Godot-specific. gitignore, staging and committing, and the basic push and pull workflow to a remote. As an example, you will see a simple folder layout that separates Scenes, Scripts, and Assets, and a. gitignore that prevents editor caches and generated import files from polluting the repository. This matters because without structure and version control, projects become hard to navigate and fragile to collaborate on. By the end, you will understand the practical benefit: fewer merge conflicts, clearer history, and an easier path to roll back when a change introduces a bug. Consider how your current project is organized and what the first small change will be to make it easier for others to join.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Overview

Why this chapter matters

Projects that begin organized and use version control scale. The visible example shows a tidy folder layout and Git commands you will use immediately. This reduces merge conflicts and keeps work reversible.

In this lesson
  • Design a consistent folder layout for Scenes, Scripts, and Assets.
  • Initialize Git and create a Godot .gitignore.
  • Use Git to commit, push, and pull while avoiding editor-specific files.
Coming up
  • Folder patterns and a hybrid approach.
  • Hands-on Git commands and examples.
  • Common mistakes and how to fix them.
Visual concept
Scenes
Scenes/ player.tscn level1.tscn ui.tscn
Scripts
Scripts/ player.gd enemy.gd ui_controller.gd
Assets
Assets/ Sprites/ Audio/ Fonts/
Quick Git snapshot
# initialize
cd path/to/MyFirstGitGame
git init

# add and commit
git add .
git commit -m "Initial project setup with basic structure and gitignore"
Starter .gitignore (Godot)

.godot/
*.import
export_presets.cfg
*.pck
*.zip
*.translation
Key Takeaway

Start with a simple, consistent folder layout and a Godot-aware .gitignore before you add assets or collaborators.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills that let you maintain and share Godot projects. First, you will establish a clear and maintainable folder structure so assets, scenes, and scripts are easy to find and consistent across teammates. This matters because clear structure reduces mistakes and speeds onboarding for new collaborators. Second, you will understand core version control principles and why Git stores snapshots called commits instead of full copies, enabling safe reversion and branching. A concrete example is reverting to a commit before a buggy change rather than trying to undo edits manually. Third, you will initialize a Git repository and perform basic operations like adding, committing, and checking status; you will see how small, descriptive commits make history useful. Fourth, you will configure a. gitignore file with Godot-specific entries so editor caches and generated import files are not tracked. Forgetting to ignore these files commonly causes merge conflicts; learning to exclude them saves time. Each objective combines a definition, a short example, and a practical reason you should adopt the practice.

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Objectives — Practice
Skills to practice
  • Initialize a repo with git init and create a meaningful first commit message.
  • Create and verify a .gitignore that includes .godot/ and *.import so team-specific files are excluded.
  • Use git status to confirm the working tree is clean after committing.
  • Push the initial branch to a remote and pull before starting new work to minimize conflicts.
Quick check
After following the steps, run git status. A clean result shows "nothing to commit, working tree clean." If you see generated .import files listed, revisit your .gitignore entries.

screens.title: Why a deliberate project structure matters
screens.narratorSegment: A deliberate project structure is the set of conventions you choose to organize files, and it matters because it reduces cognitive load for you and your teammates. In Godot, files include scenes, scripts, textures, audio, and fonts. If these are scattered in the root or named inconsistently, you and collaborators will waste time searching for the correct file, and automated tools or build steps become brittle. A simple definition: project structure is a human-readable map that groups related files together. For example, a small project might use top-level folders named Scenes, Scripts, and Assets, with Assets further divided into Sprites, Audio, and Fonts. This example shows the structure is discoverable and scales as you add more characters or levels. A common misconception is that structure should be minimal and flat to save time; in practice a modest hierarchy provides clarity and prevents clutter as projects grow. Another risk is over-designing a structure that no one follows; consistency matters more than complexity. Takeaway: pick a clear scheme early, document it in a README, and adapt it only when a concrete need arises. How would you map your current scenes and scripts into a tidy top-level layout?

keyIdea.title: Structure reduces friction
keyIdea.text: Grouping by purpose or feature makes files predictable and reduces wasted time searching or fixing misplaced assets.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Project Structure
Definition

A project structure groups files by role or feature to make the project navigable and maintainable over time.

Why this prevents problems
  • Faster onboarding: new team members find assets without asking.
  • Reduced accidental edits: related files are co-located.
  • Simpler automation: build or export scripts can rely on known paths.
Common misconception
A flat layout is not always simpler. For medium projects, a small, logical hierarchy scales better than a single folder with dozens of files.
Example layout
MyFirstGitGame/ Scenes/ player.tscn level1.tscn Scripts/ player.gd enemy.gd Assets/ Sprites/ player_idle.png Audio/ sfx_jump.wav Fonts/ ui_font.tres Utils/ global.gd .gitignore
Feature grouping
Group files that implement a single feature together, such as player or enemy folders.
Type grouping
Group by file type like Scenes, Scripts, and Assets for clearer navigation across the whole project.

screens.title: Common folder patterns for Godot projects
screens.narratorSegment: There are three common folder patterns you will encounter: type-based, feature-based, and a hybrid. Type-based organizes by kind of asset — Scenes, Scripts, and Assets. This is easy to browse when you know the type of the file you need. Feature-based groups everything that implements a feature together, such as a Player folder containing player scene, player scripts, and player sprites. This approach is useful when features are developed by small teams or iteratively. A hybrid approach combines both: top-level folders for Scenes and Scripts while Assets are split into Sprites, Audio, and Fonts, and certain features also have their own folders when complex. Concrete example: keep Scenes/player. tscn, Scripts/player. gd, and Assets/Sprites/player_idle. png, but create Assets/Player/ when the player has many specialized sprites and audio. A misconception is to rigidly follow one pattern for every project; instead, align your structure to the project's scope and the team's workflow. Practically, agree on conventions early and document them. Your task after this lesson is to describe which pattern fits your current project and why. Common folder patterns for Godot projects means choose a type, feature, or hybrid pattern that fits your project's scale and team, then write it down so everyone follows the same rules.. In practical terms, type-based, feature-based, and hybrid approaches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Folder Patterns
Type-based
Organize by Scenes, Scripts, and Assets. Simple to navigate when you know what you want.
Feature-based
Group files by feature, such as Player, Enemy, or UI, useful when features are self-contained.
Hybrid
Combine both: maintain top-level Scenes and Scripts while allowing feature folders for complex areas.
Concrete example
Assets/ Sprites/ player_idle.png Player/ player_run_sheet.png Scenes/ player.tscn Scripts/ player.gd
When the player has many specialized assets, move them into a Player subfolder under Assets while keeping scenes and core scripts at a predictable top level.

screens.title: Singletons and the Utils / Global folder
screens.narratorSegment: Singletons, often called autoloads in Godot, are scripts loaded at startup and used across your game. It's common to keep these in a dedicated Utils or Global folder so they are easy to locate and not scattered among feature folders. For example, a global. gd might hold game state like player lives or a settings manager; placing it at Utils/global. gd makes its purpose obvious. A clear practice is to group autoloads separately because they will be referenced by many scenes and scripts; mixing them into feature folders makes them harder to find and increases coupling. A common misconception is that globals should be avoided entirely; while overusing globals harms modularity, well-scoped singletons for truly global concerns simplify access and reduce repetitive code. If you use singletons, document their A P I and list them in a README so new contributors know what global state exists. Takeaway: reserve a consistent folder for autoload scripts and keep their responsibilities narrow to avoid hidden dependencies that make refactoring costly. Singletons and the Utils / Global folder means keep singletons in a utils or global folder with narrow responsibilities so they are discoverable and easier to maintain.. In practical terms, where to place global scripts and why consistency matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Keep singletons in a Utils or Global folder with narrow responsibilities so they are discoverable and easier to maintain.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Autoloads
What is an autoload?

An autoload is a script configured to load at game startup so its functions and state are available globally.

Why a dedicated folder?
  • Discoverability: contributors find globals quickly.
  • Low coupling: keep global state minimal and well-documented.
  • Refactor safety: grouped singletons are easier to replace or test.
Example
Utils/ global.gd # autoload for settings and state audio_manager.gd # singleton for SFX and music control # In project settings, autoload these scripts so they are available everywhere
Pro tip
Keep autoload responsibilities narrow. If a script grows large, consider splitting it and only autoload what truly needs global access.

screens.title: Initializing Git in a Godot project
screens.narratorSegment: Initializing a Git repository in your Godot project is the first step to recording your work. Begin in the terminal by changing directory to your project's root. Run git init to create a new repository. This command sets up Git metadata but does not yet track any files. Next, add a. gitignore file with Godot-specific entries so generated and editor-specific files are not tracked. Then stage the files you intend to track. Using git add. stages all unignored files; alternatively, git add path/to/file limits the staging to specific files when you want precision. A concrete example: after creating the Scenes, Scripts, and Assets folders and adding a README and. gitignore, run git add. followed by git commit -m "Initial project setup with basic structure and gitignore". A frequent misconception is that git init automatically tracks everything; it does not. Another is that deleting generated files before committing is required — instead, add them to. gitignore so Git ignores them going forward. Final question to consider: what commit message will make the project history most useful for you in three months?

keyIdea.title: Init, ignore, add, commit
keyIdea.text: Initialize the repo, configure .gitignore, stage the right files, and write a descriptive first commit message.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Git Init
Terminal walkthrough
cd path/to/MyFirstGitGame
# create repository
git init

# create .gitignore and add rules
# stage files (only unignored files)
git add .

# commit with a descriptive message
git commit -m "Initial project setup with basic structure and gitignore"
Staging all files with git add . is convenient, but when you need precision, stage files individually. Small, focused commits make history easier to read and revert.
Checklist
  • Run git init in project root.
  • Create .gitignore before staging files.
  • Use clear commit messages for the initial setup.

screens.title: .gitignore essentials for Godot
screens.narratorSegment: The. gitignore file instructs Git which files and folders to ignore. For Godot projects, certain patterns are essential because Godot creates editor-specific cache files and generated import files that differ between machines. A minimal Godot. gitignore includes. godot/ to skip the editor cache and settings directory, and *. import to ignore generated import metadata. It’s also common to ignore export presets and exported packages like *. pck or *. zip, and translation artifacts such as *. translation. A concrete example of a. gitignore was provided and should be placed at the repository root. A common misconception is to selectively delete generated files before committing; that’s unnecessary and fragile because Godot will regenerate them. Instead, add the right ignore patterns so these files never enter version history. Another small risk is accidentally committing. godot/ which quickly leads to merge conflicts because editor settings differ per developer. After creating. gitignore, run git status to verify only intended files remain staged. Your immediate action should be to add. gitignore before the first commit. .gitignore essentials for Godot means include .godot/, *.import, export_presets.cfg, and package files so only source assets and scripts are tracked.. In practical terms, entries that keep your repository clean and conflict-free. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › .gitignore
Recommended .gitignore
# Godot-specific ignores
.godot/
*.import
export_presets.cfg
*.pck
*.zip
*.translation
Place this file at the project root before running your first git add. After adding it, run git status to confirm generated files are no longer shown as untracked.
Common mistake
Committing .godot/ causes frequent, noisy merge conflicts because project settings are often user-specific. Always ignore it unless your team intentionally shares editor settings.

screens.title: Staging, committing, and writing useful messages
screens.narratorSegment: Staging and committing are the core of how Git records snapshots. Staging with git add prepares specific changes for the next commit. Committing records those staged changes with a message describing why the change was made. Best practice is to commit small, logically-related changes with a descriptive message. For example, after adding a player scene and its script, a single commit message like Initial player scene and script explains the purpose. Avoid mixing unrelated changes, such as adding a texture and refactoring code, in one commit; that makes future reverts harder. The concrete commands are git add path/to/file to stage specific files, git commit -m "message" to create the commit, and git status to verify the working tree. A common misconception is that fewer commits are cleaner; in reality, small commits are more useful for debugging because you can revert or cherry-pick specific changes. Closing takeaway: write messages that answer what changed and why, and keep each commit focused enough that a single change can be isolated from history. In practical terms, capture small, descriptive commits so history stays readable and reversible. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Staging & Commits
Step sequence
  1. Make focused changes in the editor or code.
  2. Stage specific files with git add path/to/file.
  3. Commit with git commit -m "Descriptive message".
  4. Run git status to ensure the working tree is clean.
git add Scripts/player.gd git commit -m "Add player movement and jump mechanics"
Misconception
Large commits are not inherently better. They make it hard to find when a specific change introduced a bug. Prefer small, focused commits with clear messages.

screens.title: Using remotes: push, pull, and collaborate
screens.narratorSegment: A remote repository hosted on services like GitHub or GitLab is how teams share code and collaborate. After creating a remote repository, link it locally with git remote add origin followed by the repository URL. Push your initial branch with git push -u origin main so the remote gets the history. When collaborating, always pull the latest changes before you start new work using git pull origin main to reduce merge conflicts. screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.narratorSegment: Teams often run into the same problems when first using Git with Godot. The most common mistake is tracking editor caches like the. godot directory or generated import files. This leads to frequent merge conflicts because these files change per user and per machine. The correct approach is to add. godot/ and *. import to. gitignore so these files are never tracked. Another frequent error is not pulling before pushing; this results in rejected pushes or surprise merges. The habit to avoid this is to git pull origin main before starting a feature. A third mistake is large, unfocused commits that mix unrelated changes; avoid that by staging specific files and making logical commits. fullNarratorScript:
Today we take two essential steps that keep a game project healthy over time. First, you will learn how to organize Godot project files so you and your team can find scenes, assets, and scripts quickly. A consistent layout prevents confusion, reduces accidental edits, and speeds development. Second, you will learn how to use Git to record your project's history, share work with others, and recover from mistakes. We’ll walk through initializing a repository, configuring a Godot-specific. gitignore, staging and committing, and the basic push and pull workflow to a remote. As an example, you will see a simple folder layout that separates Scenes, Scripts, and Assets, and a. gitignore that prevents editor caches and generated import files from polluting the repository. This matters because without structure and version control, projects become hard to navigate and fragile to collaborate on. By the end, you will understand the practical benefit: fewer merge conflicts, clearer history, and an easier path to roll back when a change introduces a bug. Consider how your current project is organized and what the first small change will be to make it easier for others to join.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical skills that let you maintain and share Godot projects. First, you will establish a clear and maintainable folder structure so assets, scenes, and scripts are easy to find and consistent across teammates. This matters because clear structure reduces mistakes and speeds onboarding for new collaborators. Second, you will understand core version control principles and why Git stores snapshots called commits instead of full copies, enabling safe reversion and branching. A concrete example is reverting to a commit before a buggy change rather than trying to undo edits manually. Third, you will initialize a Git repository and perform basic operations like adding, committing, and checking status; you will see how small, descriptive commits make history useful. Fourth, you will configure a. gitignore file with Godot-specific entries so editor caches and generated import files are not tracked. Forgetting to ignore these files commonly causes merge conflicts; learning to exclude them saves time. Each objective combines a definition, a short example, and a practical reason you should adopt the practice.

Continuing the objectives, you will learn hands-on steps to initialize Git in a new Godot project, create a robust. gitignore file, and perform the first commit. Practically, this means creating the repository in your project's root, staging the relevant files, and committing a descriptive message so history is meaningful. You will also learn the collaboration basics: adding a remote repository, pushing your initial branch, and pulling changes from teammates. A concrete example is pushing to a shared repository after the first commit so others can clone and contribute. We also cover why you should avoid tracking Godot's editor cache and generated import files, because they are machine-specific and will cause unnecessary conflicts. Finally, you will practice verifying the repository state with git status to ensure the working tree is clean. Each objective emphasizes a small habit — small commits, clear messages, and a correct. gitignore — that compounds into a stable collaboration workflow.

A deliberate project structure is the set of conventions you choose to organize files, and it matters because it reduces cognitive load for you and your teammates. In Godot, files include scenes, scripts, textures, audio, and fonts. If these are scattered in the root or named inconsistently, you and collaborators will waste time searching for the correct file, and automated tools or build steps become brittle. A simple definition: project structure is a human-readable map that groups related files together. For example, a small project might use top-level folders named Scenes, Scripts, and Assets, with Assets further divided into Sprites, Audio, and Fonts. This example shows the structure is discoverable and scales as you add more characters or levels. A common misconception is that structure should be minimal and flat to save time; in practice a modest hierarchy provides clarity and prevents clutter as projects grow. Another risk is over-designing a structure that no one follows; consistency matters more than complexity. Takeaway: pick a clear scheme early, document it in a README, and adapt it only when a concrete need arises. How would you map your current scenes and scripts into a tidy top-level layout?

There are three common folder patterns you will encounter: type-based, feature-based, and a hybrid. Type-based organizes by kind of asset — Scenes, Scripts, and Assets. This is easy to browse when you know the type of the file you need. Feature-based groups everything that implements a feature together, such as a Player folder containing player scene, player scripts, and player sprites. This approach is useful when features are developed by small teams or iteratively. A hybrid approach combines both: top-level folders for Scenes and Scripts while Assets are split into Sprites, Audio, and Fonts, and certain features also have their own folders when complex. Concrete example: keep Scenes/player. tscn, Scripts/player. gd, and Assets/Sprites/player_idle. png, but create Assets/Player/ when the player has many specialized sprites and audio. Singletons, often called autoloads in Godot, are scripts loaded at startup and used across your game. It's common to keep these in a dedicated Utils or Global folder so they are easy to locate and not scattered among feature folders. For example, a global. gd might hold game state like player lives or a settings manager; placing it at Utils/global. gd makes its purpose obvious. A clear practice is to group autoloads separately because they will be referenced by many scenes and scripts; mixing them into feature folders makes them harder to find and increases coupling.
